title: Living in Bhutan | How People Live in the Most Isolated Nation in Asia | 4K
fullText: In the highest mountain range on earth, folded into the deep valleys and steep ridges of the eastern Himalayas, lies a small and quiet kingdom. For centuries, it remained a mystery to the outside world. A nation intentionally [music] shielded by its formidable geography and its own deliberate choice. It is a land of clean air, of ancient forests, of rivers the color of glacial melt, and of a silence that is broken only by the wind, the call of a raven, or the distant chime of a monastery bell. This is Bhutan, the last Himalayan kingdom, known to its people as Druul, the land of the thunder dragon. From the air, it appears as a formidable landscape of green and white. A seemingly endless ocean of mountains, their peaks scraping the sky. It is a vertical world where flat land is a precious rarity and where life has adapted to the contours of the earth with patience and ingenuity. The very air here feels different, thin, crisp, and carrying the scent of pine and damp [music] earth. But to look closer is to discover a society built not on the conquest of the landscape but on a deep and abiding harmony with it. This is a nation where success is measured not by material wealth but by collective happiness. Where ancient traditions are not relics of the past but the living breathing fabric of the present. and where spirituality is woven into the very warp and weft of daily existence. This is the story of a people whose lives are shaped by the mountains that protect them, the faith that guides them and the quiet strength of a community that holds them together. This is the story of life in Bhutan. Life in Bhutan is governed by the rhythm of the seasons and the steady unhurried pace of the mountains. The population is small, less than a million people scattered across a country the size of Switzerland. This fosters a profound sense of intimacy [music] and interconnectedness. In the small towns and villages that form the heart of the nation, anonymity is an unfamiliar concept. Life is lived in public among faces that have been known since birth, connected by intricate webs of family and shared history. Even in the capital city, Thimfu, which nestles in a long, narrow valley, the atmosphere is more of an overgrown town than a bustling metropolis. It is a capital city with no traffic lights where policemen direct [music] the modest flow of vehicles with graceful stylized hand gestures from a decorated booth in the center of an intersection. A human touch in a world of automation. The landscape itself dictates the structure of life. Villages are often clustered on the rare patches of gentle slope. Their houses built to withstand the elements and to reflect a deep cultural aesthetic. Traditional Bhutanese architecture is a defining feature of the kingdom. Sturdy timber framed houses with [music] brightly painted window frames, sloping roofs, and a distinctive inward sloping profile. [music] These homes are not just shelters. They are sanctuaries of family life, often housing multiple generations under one roof. The walls are constructed from rammed earth or stone providing insulation against the cold winters and the summer heat. The intricate wooden cornes and window frames are painted with traditional motifs, dragons, flowers, and auspicious symbols, each telling a story. The day begins early, not with the sound of traffic, but with the first light touching the mountain peaks, the low chant of a morning [music] prayer, or the crowing of a rooster. Life moves with a deliberate mindful quality, a pace that seems to be set by the mountains themselves, ancient, [music] patient, and enduring. The cornerstone of Bhutanese society is the family and the village. In the rural communities where the majority of the population still lives, daily life is a collective endeavor anchored in [music] the cycles of agriculture. The routines are simple, dependable, and tied to the earth. For farmers, the day [music] is a conversation with the land. It begins with tending to the livestock, [music] a cow for milk, a few chickens for eggs, and then moves to the fields. Depending on the altitude and the season, this could mean planting rice in the meticulously terrace patties of the lower valleys, a backbreaking process of transplanting bright green seedlings by hand into the flooded earth. In higher valleys like Bumang, it means harvesting potatoes or buckwheat. Their pale flowers are stark contrast to the deep [music] green of the surrounding forests. The family unit is strong and resilient with grandparents, parents, and children often living and working together. This creates a [music] powerful support system where wisdom is passed down from one generation to the next. Not in classrooms, but in the fields and around the hearth. Grandparents care for the young children, [music] telling them ancient stories of demons and saints, while the parents manage the heavy work of the farm. Homes are centers of warmth and activity. The kitchen is the heart of the house. A place for cooking, for sharing meals, and for gathering on cold nights around a traditional wood burning [music] stove, the Bkari. The air is thick with the smell of wood smoke and the bubbling of the day's meal. This inherent closeness extends beyond the family to the entire village. Community life is built on an unspoken understanding of mutual responsibility. When it is time to plant or harvest, families work on each other's fields in turn. A system that ensures no one is left behind. When a new house is built, the entire village comes together to help. A practice known as Tessa Dronam. Men work on the heavy timber framing and [music] stone masonry while women carry materials and provide food and drink for the workers. The air is filled with a spirit of cooperation and celebration. There is a deep-seated belief that the well-being of the individual is inseparable from the well-being of the community. This interdependence is not seen as a burden but as a source of strength [music] and security. A social safety net woven from generations of shared experience and [music] mutual trust. To understand Bhutan is to understand the central role of Vajreana Buddhism. It is not simply a religion. It is the foundation of the nation's identity, its culture, its laws, and its [music] art. The landscape is dotted with sacred sites, monasteries perched precariously [music] on cliffs, ancient temples, and small shrines known as chortans that house religious relics. Prayer flags are a ubiquitous [music] and beautiful site. There are five colors representing the five elements. Blue for the sky, white for the air, red for fire, green for water, and yellow for the earth. They are strung across bridges on high mountain passes. And from the roofs of houses carrying prayers and blessings on the wind, the mantras on them slowly fading as they release their goodwill into the world. The spiritual and administrative heart of each district is the Zong, a magnificent and imposing fortress monastery. These architectural marvels built without a single nail or architectural plan serve as the center of government, the head of the local monastic body and a symbol of Bhutanese identity. Inside their high whitewashed walls, monks in saffron and crimson robes perform ancient rituals that have remained unchanged for centuries. Their deep guttural chants echoing [music] through the courtyards. These are not museums. They are living working centers of faith and governance. This spiritual heritage is a living tradition. Monks are a respected and integral part of every [music] community. Families often send one of their sons to a monastery, considering it an honor and a way to accumulate merit. The national dress is another powerful and visible symbol of this unique identity. Men wear the go, a kneelength robe tied at the waist with a belt called a kira forming a large pouch at the front used for carrying everything [music] from a mobile phone to a small bowl. Women wear the Kira, an elegant floorlength rectangular cloth [music] wrapped around the body and secured at the shoulders with ornate brooches, often worn with a silk jacket [music] called a toiggo. It is not a costume for special occasions. It is everyday attire worn with pride in schools, [music] government offices, and on the street. This shared cultural language is a cornerstone of the national philosophy of [music] gross national happiness. A unique development model that prioritizes the well-being of the people based on the four pillars of sustainable development, environmental protection, cultural preservation, and good governance over pure economic growth. For generations, the Bhutanese economy was almost [music] entirely self-sufficient, based on subsistence farming and barter. Today, while agriculture remains the primary occupation for the majority of the population, the economy is slowly and carefully modernizing. In the high altitude regions like the remote village of Lia, yak hering is a way of life. The layups, a semi-nomadic people, move their herds to different pastures depending on the season. Their lives a testament to human adaptation in an extreme environment. The yak provides everything. Meat, milk for cheese and butter, thick wool for clothing and tents, and its strength for transport. In the fertile lower valleys, rice is the staple crop. Its cultivation a demanding laborintensive process that shapes the entire year. [music] The largest driver of the modern economy is hydro power. The country's fast flowing rivers fed by Himalayan glacias are a source of clean renewable energy. The vast majority of which is sold to neighboring India providing the government with its primary source of revenue. This income funds the country's free education and health care systems [music] cornerstones of the gross national happiness philosophy. Government jobs are highly sought after providing stability and a good salary in a country with limited private sector opportunities. Tourism is another important though carefully managed sector. Bhutan has famously pursued a policy of high value low impact tourism. A mandatory sustainable development fee for visitors ensures that the number of tourists remains manageable. preventing the kind of over tourism that has affected other parts of the world. This approach aims to protect the country's unique culture [music] and pristine environment while generating revenue that benefits local communities. It means that those who visit are often deeply interested in the culture and their interactions are more meaningful. Alongside these larger sectors, a small but growing number of entrepreneurs are starting their own businesses. From guest houses and restaurants to smallcale craft production of textiles and incense, slowly diversifying the economic landscape. [music] Bhutanese food is a direct reflection of its mountain environment. Hearty, simple, and often intensely spicy. The cuisine is built around a few core ingredients that can be grown in the challenging climate. The undisputed national dish eaten everyday in almost every household is emadachi. The name is simple. Imma means chili and dachi means cheese. It is a fiery stewike curry made from hot chilies, sometimes split lengthwise, sometimes chopped, and a local farmer's cheese that melts into a creamy pungent sauce. It is a dish that warms the body and soul in the cool mountain air. Chilies are not used as a seasoning in Bhutan. They are treated [music] as a vegetable. At any local market, from the large centenerary farmers market in Thimfu to a small village gathering, you will see piles of red and green chilies, both fresh and dried. The air is thick with their sharp, earthy scent. Red rice is the staple grain, a nutritious, nutty flavored [music] variety that grows in the high altitudes. It forms the base of almost every meal. Served alongside one or two [music] stewike dishes. Its pinkish hue and firm texture are a perfect counterpoint to the rich spicy curries. Other common ingredients include potatoes, turnips, and buckwheat, which is used to make noodles and savory [music] pancakes, especially in the Bumthang region. Pork is a favored meat often cooked with giant white radishes in a dish called faka pa. The traditional drink is suja or butter tea. A salty savory beverage made by churning tea, salt, [music] and yak butter together. It is an acquired taste for outsiders, but for the Bhutanese, it provides warmth and vital calories for a hard day's work in the mountains. Food culture is centered in the home. Meals are a simple communal [music] affair, a time for family to gather, share the food that they have often grown themselves, and reconnect at the end of the day. To live in Bhutan is to live in intimate daily contact with nature. The landscape is not a backdrop. [music] It is an active and powerful presence. The country is one of the few in the world that is carbon negative, meaning its vast forests absorb more carbon dioxide than the country produces. The constitution mandates that at least 60% of the country must remain under forest cover for all time, a testament to the nation's deep commitment to environmental preservation. This is not just a policy. It is a reflection of the Buddhist belief in the sacredness of all life. Life is lived outdoors. For centuries, the only way to travel between valleys was on [music] foot along a network of trails that crisscross the country. Hiking and walking are not just recreational activities. They are a fundamental part of life. These trails lead through dense pine and roodendran forests, across high mountain passes adorned with prayer flags, [music] and down into serene hidden valleys. The experience of walking these paths is immersive. The springy feel of pine needles underfoot, the sudden reveal of a snowcapped peak, the sound of a distant monastery horn. The landscape is varied and dramatic. In the south, subtropical forests are home to a rich diversity of wildlife, including tigers, elephants, and the rare golden langu. [music] In the central valleys, rivers have carved out fertile basins where rice terraces [music] climb the hillsides like giant green staircases. In the north, one finds the high Himalayas, a world of alpine meadows, glacial lakes, and towering snowcovered peaks that are considered the sacred abode of the gods. Here in villages that are among the highest human settlements on earth, life is a testament to human resilience. The connection to this land is profound. It is a source of sustenance, a place of spiritual power and an integral part of the Putin identity. For all its timeless qualities, Bhutan is a country in transition. For centuries, its geography enforced its isolation. Today, a network of roads painstakingly carved into the mountainsides connects the major towns. Travel is slow and often arduous. A journey of 100 km can take several hours as the road twists and turns, climbs high passes, and descends into deep valleys. Landslides during the monsoon season can close roads for days, a constant reminder of the power of nature. These journeys, however, are part of the experience, marked by stops for tea at small roadside stalls and breathtaking views at every turn. Modernization is most visible in [music] the capital Timu. Here, one finds a growing number of modern [music] buildings, restaurants, and shops, all still required to incorporate traditional architectural elements. The internet and the smartphone have become a part [music] of daily life, connecting even remote villages to the outside world. This influx of technology and global culture presents one of the central paradoxes of modern Bhutan. It is now possible to see a monk in ancient robes checking his messages on a smartphone or to find young people in a traditional village wearing the latest global fashions alongside their go and kiraas. This blending of the old and the new is a defining feature of contemporary Bhutanese life. The country was one of the last in the world to introduce television and the internet doing so only in 1999. The government and the people are engaged in a constant thoughtful negotiation. How to embrace the benefits of modernity such as improved health care and education without sacrificing the unique culture and traditions that define them. It is a delicate dance between preservation and progress. For the young people of Bhutan, life is a unique blend of ancient tradition and global influence. Education is a high priority for the government and is provided free [music] to all citizens. The school system is a bridge between two [music] worlds. The curriculum is modern, taught in English, preparing students for a connected world. Yet the traditional language Zonga is also taught and students wear a version of the national dress as their uniform, instilling a strong [music] sense of cultural identity from a young age. In the mornings, [music] schoolyards across the country echo with the sound of the national anthem, a reminder of their shared heritage. For many young people, growing up in a small remote village, the path to higher education or employment [music] leads to the larger towns, particularly Thimfu. This migration is a modern right of passage, a journey from the quiet, predictable world of the village to the more dynamic and complex environment of the city. It is a time of new opportunities, but also of new challenges as they learn to navigate a world [music] that is faster and more individualistic than the one they left behind. [music] The great task for Bhutan's youth is to navigate this dual reality. They are connected to global youth culture through their smartphones, listening to the same music, and watching the same movies as their peers around the world. At the same time they are deeply rooted [music] in a culture of family, community and Buddhist values. They are expected to uphold Drilam Namja, the traditional code of etiquette that governs how one should behave, dress and interact with others. The challenge for the nation is to create enough meaningful opportunities for its educated young people [music] so they can build a future at home, contributing their skills and global perspectives to the country's continued careful evolution. The rhythm of day and night in Bhutan is a study in simplicity and quietude. The day begins with the sun, and for most people, it is a time of [music] work and activity. In the monasteries, the day starts before dawn with the sound of [music] a gong or a horn calling the monks to morning prayers. In the villages, farmers are in their fields making the [music] most of the daylight hours. The towns come to life slowly with shops opening and people going about their business with a calm, unhurried demeanor. The energy is productive and grounded, a reflection of a society that lives close to the land and understands the value of hard work. As evening approaches, a profound sense of peace descends. When the sun drops [music] behind the high mountain peaks, darkness falls quickly and completely. Life turns inward. The towns and villages become still. The sounds of the day are replaced by the gentle murmur of a river, the chirping of insects, or the whisper of the wind through the pines. This is a time for home, for family. It is a time for sharing the evening meal, for conversation, for prayer. In many [music] homes, the evening includes a small ritual, the lighting of a butter lamp as an offering for the benefit of all sentient beings. The quiet nights are a cherished part of life. A time for rest and reflection. A time to restore the body and spirit. Ready for the new day. Life [music] in this serene and beautiful kingdom is not without its challenges. The geography, while stunning, presents formidable obstacles. The mountainous [music] terrain, makes farming difficult and limits the amount of arable land. Building and maintaining infrastructure like roads and power lines is a constant and costly battle against the elements. Many remote communities are still accessible only by foot, hours, or even days from the nearest road, making access to health care and markets a significant struggle. The economy while growing is small and has a narrow base, heavily reliant on hydro power sales to [music] India. Creating enough jobs for a growing well-educated young population is a significant and ongoing concern. The careful high value approach to tourism while successful in preserving culture also limits the potential for economic growth in that sector. Bhutan is also highly vulnerable to the effects of climate change. Its glacias are melting at an alarming rate, increasing [music] the risk of catastrophic glacial lake outburst floods, which could devastate entire valleys with little warning. And perhaps the most profound challenge is the one that lies at the heart of the modern Bhutanese experience. The delicate act of balancing the old and the new. How does a nation preserve its unique cultural identity, its spiritual depth, and its communal values in the face of an increasingly interconnected and globalized world. These are the questions that Bhutan is thoughtfully and collectively navigating. as it charts its course in the 21st century. [music] So why do people choose to stay in a world that offers endless possibilities? What keeps them rooted in this small remote kingdom? The answers are found not in what Bhutan has [music] but in what it is. They stay for the unshakable sense of community, for the security of knowing you belong to a place [music] where people genuinely care for one another, where a problem for one family is a problem for the whole village. They stay for the peace, for the pervasive quiet that allows for a deeper connection to oneself and to the world. They stay for the safety, for the freedom to walk anywhere at any time and for their children to grow up in an environment of trust and security. They stay for the profound spiritual heritage that gives meaning and context to life, a framework of compassion and mindfulness that is woven into the fabric of society. And above all, they stay for the deep, unbreakable connection to their home, to a landscape that is not just [music] scenery, but a sacred and living part of their identity. It is the feeling of being part of a story that is ancient, unique, and still unfolding. [music] Bhutan exists in a rare and beautiful equilibrium. A balance between the ancient and the modern, [music] between the spiritual and the practical, between the needs of the individual and the well-being of the community. It is a country shaped by the formidable power of the Himalayas and the gentle [music] enduring strength of the Buddhist faith. Here life is measured not in the rush of minutes but in the passing of seasons, not in [music] the accumulation of wealth but in the richness of family and community. It is a living testament to the idea that a nation can choose its own path. A path guided by wisdom, compassion, and a profound respect for the earth. In a world that is constantly searching for happiness, Bhutan offers a quiet reminder that perhaps it is not something to be pursued, but something to be cultivated together in the stillness of the mountains.
fullTextVi: Ở dãy núi cao nhất trái đất, lọt vào thung lũng sâu và dốc rặng núi phía đông dãy Himalaya, là một vương quốc nhỏ bé và yên tĩnh. Trong nhiều thế kỷ, nó vẫn là một bí ẩn đối với thế giới bên ngoài. Một quốc gia có chủ ý [âm nhạc] được che chắn bởi vị trí địa lý ghê gớm và sự lựa chọn có chủ ý của chính mình. Đó là vùng đất không khí trong lành, của những cánh rừng cổ thụ, của những dòng sông màu của băng tan và của sự im lặng chỉ bị phá vỡ bởi gió, tiếng quạ kêu, hay tiếng chuông xa xa của tu viện. Đây là Bhutan, vương quốc cuối cùng trên dãy Himalaya, được người dân ở đây gọi là Druul, vùng đất của rồng sấm sét. Từ trên không, nó xuất hiện như một khung cảnh ấn tượng với màu xanh và trắng. Một đại dương núi dường như vô tận, những đỉnh núi chọc thủng bầu trời. Đó là một thế giới thẳng đứng nơi đất bằng phẳng là một điều quý hiếm và là nơi cuộc sống đã thích nghi với đường nét của trái đất bằng sự kiên nhẫn và khéo léo. Không khí ở đây thật khác lạ, loãng, trong lành và mang theo mùi thông và đất [âm nhạc] ẩm ướt. Nhưng nhìn kỹ hơn là phát hiện ra một xã hội được xây dựng không phải trên sự chinh phục của cảnh quan nhưng lại có sự hòa hợp sâu sắc và lâu dài với nó. Đây là một quốc gia mà thành công được đo lường không phải bằng của cải vật chất mà bằng hạnh phúc tập thể. Nơi truyền thống xa xưa không phải là di tích của quá khứ mà là tấm vải thở sống của hiện tại. và nơi tâm linh được dệt thành sợi dọc và sợi ngang của sự tồn tại hàng ngày. Đây là câu chuyện về một dân tộc có cuộc sống được định hình bởi những ngọn núi bảo vệ họ, niềm tin hướng dẫn họ và sức mạnh thầm lặng của một cộng đồng gắn kết họ lại với nhau. Đây là câu chuyện về cuộc sống ở Bhutan. Cuộc sống ở Bhutan bị chi phối bởi nhịp điệu của các mùa và sự ổn định nhịp độ chậm rãi của núi. Dân số ít, chưa đến một triệu người sống rải rác trên khắp đất nước kích thước của Thụy Sĩ Điều này nuôi dưỡng cảm giác sâu sắc về sự gần gũi [âm nhạc] và sự kết nối với nhau. Ở những thị trấn và làng nhỏ tạo thành trái tim của đất nước, sự ẩn danh là một khái niệm xa lạ. Cuộc đời được sống công khai giữa những gương mặt đã quen từ khi sinh ra, được kết nối bởi các mạng lưới phức tạp của gia đình và lịch sử chung. Ngay cả ở thủ đô Thimfu, ẩn mình trong một thung lũng dài và hẹp, bầu không khí giống một thị trấn phát triển quá mức hơn là một đô thị nhộn nhịp. Đây là một thành phố thủ đô không có đèn giao thông, nơi cảnh sát chỉ đạo [âm nhạc] dòng xe khiêm tốn với cử chỉ tay cách điệu duyên dáng từ một gian hàng được trang trí ở tâm của một ngã tư. Một liên lạc của con người trong một thế giới tự động hóa. Bản thân cảnh quan quyết định cấu trúc của cuộc sống. Các bản làng thường tập trung trên những mảnh đất có độ dốc thoai thoải hiếm hoi. Những ngôi nhà của họ được xây dựng để chống chọi với các yếu tố thời tiết và phản ánh nét thẩm mỹ văn hóa sâu sắc. Kiến trúc truyền thống của Bhutan là đặc điểm nổi bật của vương quốc. Những ngôi nhà khung gỗ chắc chắn với khung cửa sổ [âm nhạc] được sơn màu rực rỡ, mái dốc và hồ sơ dốc vào trong đặc biệt. [âm nhạc] Những ngôi nhà này không chỉ là nơi trú ẩn. Chúng là nơi tôn nghiêm của cuộc sống gia đình, thường là nơi ở của nhiều thế hệ dưới một mái nhà. Các bức tường được xây bằng đất nện hoặc đá để cách nhiệt chống lạnh mùa đông và cái nóng mùa hè. Các góc gỗ và khung cửa sổ tinh xảo được vẽ các họa tiết truyền thống, rồng, hoa, và các biểu tượng tốt lành, mỗi biểu tượng kể một câu chuyện. Ngày bắt đầu sớm, không phải bằng tiếng xe cộ mà bằng đầu tiên ánh sáng chạm tới đỉnh núi, tiếng tụng kinh trầm của lời cầu nguyện [âm nhạc] buổi sáng hoặc tiếng gáy của gà trống. Cuộc sống chuyển động với phẩm chất chánh niệm có chủ ý, một nhịp độ dường như đã được ấn định sẵn bên những ngọn núi, cổ xưa, [âm nhạc] kiên nhẫn và bền bỉ. Nền tảng của xã hội Bhutan là gia đình và làng quê. Ở các cộng đồng nông thôn nơi phần lớn dân số vẫn sinh sống, cuộc sống hàng ngày là một nỗ lực tập thể gắn liền với [âm nhạc] các chu kỳ của nông nghiệp. segments.text: that perhaps it is not something to be pursued, but something to be cultivated
segments.viText: rằng có lẽ đó không phải là thứ để theo đuổi mà là thứ để trau dồi

segments.text: together in the stillness of the mountains.
segments.viText: cùng nhau trong sự tĩnh lặng của núi rừng.
